extracted.intended_audience: general readers of Laurence Sterne; aspiring novelists interested in metafictional/18th-century style
extracted.subtask_description: Informal, metafictional guidance and self-commentary on composing a novel: chapter composition, tone consistency, when to excise material, and stylistic choices (directness vs. ostentation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain chapter-to-chapter balance (equipoise)
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain a 'necessary equipoise and balance (whether of good or bad) betwixt chapter and chapter, from whence the just proportions and harmony of the whole work results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a passage or chapter upsets the balance of the whole (by being out of tune with surrounding material), it can depreciate other scenes and destroy the work's harmony; such material may need to be removed or altered. Example: the author tore out a chapter describing a cavalcade because it was "so much above the stile and manner of any thing else" that it would have depreciated other scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be in tune with yourself (consistent style/tone)
rubrics_metrics.description: To write a book is for all the world like humming a song—be but in tune with yourself, ’tis no matter how high or how low you take it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain an internal consistency of voice and manner. The overall acceptability of a passage depends on being 'in tune' with the author's established manner; variations in pitch (high/low) are less important than internal coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excise exceptional passages that isolate or overshadow
rubrics_metrics.description: Remove or omit material which, though excellent in itself, would be 'so perpendicular a precipice... so wholly cut off from the rest of the work' that it isolates the reader or overshadows surrounding material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An especially fine or elevated passage can be harmful if it creates an ascent or declivity inaccessible from neighboring material; the author gives the example of a passage that carried the soul 'into the other world' and thus could not be integrated back into the book without spoiling balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer directness and sincerity over display
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid preaching or writing that primarily displays erudition or wit; 'To preach, to shew the extent of our reading, or the subtleties of our wit... is a dishonest use' of time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to address the heart plainly ('direct five words point-blank to the heart') rather than parade learning. The anti-pattern is showy, glittering language that conveys little warmth or substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ornate language that 'glitters' without meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not 'parade in the eyes of the vulgar with the beggarly accounts of a little learning, tinsel'd over with a few words which glitter, but convey little light and less warmth.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize clarity and substantive feeling over rhetorical ornament; excessive glittering diction is criticized as empty and self-serving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful of satire's collateral harm
rubrics_metrics.description: When satirizing or briskly riding through topics, the writer risks "treading upon" or "splashing" real people and professions—"If you ride at this rate... you’ll do some one a mischief."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise caution in targets and scope of satire; even with good intentions to 'tread upon no one', rapid or broad satire may offend unintended individuals or groups (painters, poets, bishops, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiment with structural deletions (chapter removal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Testing removal of chapters or sections can improve the whole: 'the book is more perfect and complete by wanting the chapter, than having it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be willing to try excising chapters or passages to see if the overall book benefits; the author explicitly argues for experimenting with chapter deletion to preserve balance and proportion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sudden, isolated stylistic shifts
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not insert passages that form a 'perpendicular precipice'—an abrupt stylistic or tonal shift that separates the passage from the rest of the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such precipitous shifts create passages that readers cannot 'descend into' from neighboring material; they may feel disjointed and harm continuity. Ensure transitions and accessibility of tonal changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose fresh ('maiden') subjects to avoid clashing with established wisdom
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer 'maiden' subjects where the writer 'shall run foul of no man's wisdom or fine sayings' (example: button-holes as a lively, untouched topic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selecting uncommon or lightly-treated topics reduces risk of tripping over others' established authority and allows more original, unencumbered treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage the reader with novel author-reader relations (metafictional address)
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrator emphasizes the 'strange state of affairs between the reader and myself' and uses direct address and interruptions as a stylistic device.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metafictional asides and direct commentary to the reader can be a deliberate device; use such foregrounding of the author's relation to the reader for novelty, but be aware it changes expectations and pacing.
